title: The price–yield seesaw
objectives: Explain why bond prices fall when rates rise, with the ₹1,000 bond example.
Say why longer bonds swing more.
body_md:
When market interest rates rise, existing bonds with lower coupons become less attractive, so their prices fall. When rates fall, prices rise. That is the price–yield seesaw.

| A 5-year bond, ₹1,000 face value, 7% coupon | Price (approx.) |
| --- | --- |
| Market rates fall to 6% | ₹1,042 (gain) |
| Market rates stay at 7% | ₹1,000 |
| Market rates rise to 8% | ₹960 (loss) |

The longer the bond's maturity, the bigger the swing. That sensitivity is measured by duration (see the Evaluate lessons).
example: ₹1,000 bond, 7% coupon, 5 years left: rates fall to 6% → about ₹1,042; rates rise to 8% → about ₹960 (approximate, illustrative).
say: When rates rise, existing bond prices fall.
The longer the bond, the bigger the swing.
never: When rates rise, existing bond prices rise too.
A bond's price never moves before maturity.

Why do longer bonds swing more when rates move?
o: Their cash flows are further away, so rate changes affect their value more
Longer bonds are always lower rated
